unit.title: Plan to undertake a routine task

summary: This unit teaches you to plan a routine electrical job before anyone picks up a tool, the way a Level 3 electrician or team leader does. You will learn to read the work order, find and check the information, survey the site, choose the method and sequence, plan safety and safe isolation, and work out materials, time and cost. You will also learn to agree and communicate the plan, check progress and quality, handle problems and changes, and finish with a report and a review that makes the next plan better.

blocks.p: A **routine task** is work the trade does often: adding an outlet or a light, putting in a circuit for an air-conditioner or water heater, replacing fittings or a damaged accessory, or a planned maintenance visit. Routine does not mean careless. Most accidents, call-backs and wasted days on routine jobs come from skipped planning: the wrong circuit isolated, the wrong cable bought, a shutdown nobody was told about, a ladder where a tower was needed.

This unit is for Level 3 trainees. At this level you do more than follow a plan: you write it, explain why you chose each method, lead a small team through it and answer for the result. The notes follow a job from the work order to the review.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Understand the task
Read the work order or job card, find out exactly what is wanted, where, by when and to what standard, and get anything unclear or conflicting settled in writing before you plan.

Survey the site
Visit before you finish the plan to see the board, its spare ways and load, the cable routes, access, the hazards and the people who use the building.
Plan the method and the sequence
Break the job into steps in a safe, logical order, choose the best method for this job, and write a method statement.
Plan for safety and safe isolation
Write a risk assessment, choose controls, plan who isolates and locks off what, and choose the right access equipment and PPE.
Work out the resources
List materials with size, type and quantity, book the tools and test instruments, and estimate the time and cost.
Agree and communicate the plan
Get the plan approved, agree shutdowns and access with the client, brief the team and tell the people affected.
Lead and monitor the work
Give each person tasks they can do safely, check progress against the schedule and check quality at hold points.
Handle problems and changes
Stop, make safe and report when something unexpected turns up; get every change priced, agreed and recorded before you do it.
Finish, report and review
Inspect and test, update the records, hand over with a completion report, and review the job so the next plan is better.

ul: JPS supplies most homes and businesses at **110 V and 220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**. Larger buildings may have a three-phase supply. Every item you plan to buy must match the supply it will be connected to.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**. Drawings and equipment use both US and British words: ground and earth, panel and board, GFCI and RCD. Plan to the code edition and the specification that the job uses.

A new or altered installation is inspected by a **licensed electrical inspector**, under the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)**, before JPS will connect or reconnect it. When a job needs that inspection, the plan must allow time for it.

Heat in roof spaces, the rainy seasons, the hurricane season and power cuts all affect timing and safety. Many buildings also have standby generators, solar PV or UPS units that can keep a circuit live after you switch it off.

blocks.note: This unit is part of the NCTVET Level 3 qualification in Electrical Installation and Maintenance. Your assessor will expect to see your plan in writing, and will ask you to explain why you chose each step. A plan that only exists in your head cannot be checked, shared or improved.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a real job. Work through the examples with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, even when you got the answer right. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own forms.

sections.title: Understanding the task and its priority

blocks.p: Every plan starts with a clear task. Before you plan anything, you should be able to answer six questions: **what** exactly is wanted, **where**, **why**, **by when**, **to what standard**, and **who** approves it. If you cannot answer one of them, ask before you go further. A plan built on a guess is still a guess.

blocks.h: Checking the load before you add to a circuit

blocks.p: Never add outlets or equipment to a circuit without finding out what it already feeds. Power, voltage and current are linked: **power (W) = voltage (V) × current (A)**, so **current = power ÷ voltage (I = P ÷ V)**.

**Example.** A 20 A, 110 V circuit already feeds a 1,200 W microwave and a 150 W refrigerator: 1,350 ÷ 110 = **12.3 A**. A photocopier of 1,100 W would add 1,100 ÷ 110 = 10.0 A, making 22.3 A. That is more than the breaker allows, so the plan needs a new circuit, not two more outlets on the old one.
**Example at 220 V.** A water heater rated 3,300 W at 220 V draws 3,300 ÷ 220 = **15 A**. A 220 V load is fed through a **two-pole breaker**, which switches both line conductors together.

blocks.note: The NEC, on which Jamaica's code is based, treats a load that runs at its maximum for 3 hours or more, such as a water heater, shop lighting or a room of computers, as a **continuous load**. A breaker may carry only **80%** of its rating in continuous load: no more than 16 A on a 20 A breaker. Use the rules the designer or your instructor gives you for the job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: The maker says

rows: 'Connect to a dedicated circuit'

'Maximum fuse or breaker 25 A'

'Minimum circuit ampacity 16 A' (often on air-conditioners)
The cable must be rated to carry at least 16 A.
Check it matches the Jamaican supply before it is bought or connected.
'Install a disconnect within sight of the unit'

blocks.p: Sometimes the specification says one thing and the drawing another, or the client asks for something the specification does not allow. Do not choose for yourself. Write down the conflict, send it to the person who can decide (the designer, your supervisor or the client), and get the answer **in writing** before you buy materials or start work. On bigger jobs this is called a **request for information (RFI)**. Record who decided and when.

blocks.note: On a large contract, the contract itself says which document wins when two disagree. On small jobs, nobody may have thought about it. Either way, the person who planned the job is the one who asks; a trainee on the tools should not have to guess.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Jobs compete for the same people and time. Put danger first, then loss of an important service, then improvements.

head: Priority

blocks.note: A faded or wrong board schedule looks like a low-priority job, but it is a safety matter: the next person may isolate the wrong circuit. Plan to correct it soon.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **site survey** (site visit) is a visit made before the plan is finished, to see and measure the real conditions. It is looking, measuring and asking, not working: you do not open a board, remove a cover or switch anything off unless you are authorised to and the precautions are in place.

blocks.p: Record the survey with a sketch, measurements and photos. A good sketch shows the board, every new point, the route and the length of each part, so anyone can price and plan from it.

blocks.note: Measure the route the cable will really take, not the straight line across the floor plan. A cable from a board to an outlet 6 m away across a room may need 12 m once it goes up the wall, across the ceiling and down again.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When the site does not match the drawing

blocks.p: Buildings change after drawings are made. When you find a difference, plan from what is really there, report the difference to your supervisor or the designer, agree what to do, and mark it on the drawing so the record can be corrected. Never plan from a drawing you know is wrong, and never quietly ignore it either: the next person will trust it.

sections.title: Planning the method and the sequence

blocks.p: The **method statement** breaks the job into steps, puts them in a safe order and says how each one is done, by whom and with what. At Level 3 you should be able to say why you chose each method, and write the reason down.

blocks.h: A typical sequence: a new 220 V air-conditioning circuit

flow: Read the work order and the unit's data plate and installation guide
Survey: board space, spare capacity, route, position of the outdoor unit and its isolator
Choose the cable, breaker and isolator; list materials; estimate time and cost
Agree the date and the shutdown with the client; get the plan approved
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead
First fix: fix the isolator and boxes, run conduit, draw in the cable
Second fix: terminate at the isolator and in the board
Inspect and carry out the dead tests
Energise, carry out live checks and commission the unit with the installer
Update the board schedule, clean up, report and hand over

blocks.h: Steps that depend on each other

blocks.p: Some steps must follow one another: boxes are fixed before cables are pulled, cables are pulled before they are terminated, terminations are finished before testing, and dead tests are passed before anything is switched on. Other steps can happen at the same time: one trainee can fix boxes in one room while another pulls cable in the next. Knowing which steps depend on which lets you plan the shortest safe order and keep everyone busy.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: First fix (rough-in)
Installing boxes, conduit and cables before walls and ceilings are finished.
Second fix (trim-out, final fix)
Connecting switches, outlets, fittings and the board after the finishes are done.
Make good
Repair the surfaces you disturbed, such as chases and holes, so they are neat again and ready for paint.
Hold point
A step where work stops until someone inspects or approves it, for example before a ceiling is closed over new cables.
Commissioning
Setting up equipment and proving it works as intended, often with the maker's or installer's checklist.
Contingency
Spare time (or money) in the plan for problems that usually turn up.

blocks.p: Schools, clinics, offices and shops cannot stop for your job. Plan the work in **stages** so that only one room or circuit is dead at a time and the rest of the building keeps working. Do noisy and dusty work, such as drilling and chasing, when rooms are empty. Leave each stage safe at the end of the day: no exposed live parts, no loose cables in walkways, every box closed or covered.

sections.title: Planning for safety and safe isolation

blocks.p: The **risk assessment** lists the hazards of each step, who could be harmed and how, and the controls you will use. Choose controls from the top of the hierarchy down: **eliminate** (work dead), **substitute** (battery tools instead of mains tools outdoors), **engineering controls** (barriers, guards, dust extraction), **administrative controls** (procedures, permits, signs, timing) and, last, **PPE**.

head: Hazard

Work dead with a written isolation plan; check for other sources of supply; insulated tools; no live work as routine
Work at height
The right access equipment for the height and the length of the task; trained users; never improvised platforms
Heat in roof spaces and under zinc roofs
Work early in the morning; short spells with breaks; drinking water; fans or ventilation; a partner who can see you
Hidden cables and pipes when drilling or chasing
Drawings, a cable and pipe detector, and avoiding the zones in line with existing accessories
Dust and noise from chasing and drilling
Dust extraction; eye, ear and dust protection and gloves; doing it when rooms are empty
Manual handling
Drum stands for cable, two people for long ladders and heavy fittings
Occupants and the public
Barriers and signs; tools and cables out of walkways; ladders never left standing alone
Working alone or out of hours
Someone nearby or a check-in by phone; access, keys and first aid arranged in advance

blocks.note: Heat exhaustion is a real risk in Jamaican roof spaces, which can pass 45 °C in the afternoon. Warning signs: heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, cramps and confusion. Get the person out into a cool place, give water and get help. Plan roof-space work for the cooler hours.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The isolation plan answers: **which circuit** (found on the schedule and confirmed by testing), **where** it is isolated, **who** locks it off and with whose locks, **how** it is proved dead and with which tester, and **who** may remove the locks. Writing it down stops the most common fatal mistake in routine work: someone working on a circuit they believe is dead.

flow: Identify the circuit from the schedule, then confirm it by testing
Agree the shutdown time and tell everyone affected
Switch off at the planned isolation point
Fit a lock-off device and your own padlock; keep the key
Fix a danger tag: name, date, reason, how to reach you
Prove the tester on a proving unit
Test at the point of work between all conductors, and each to earth
Prove the tester again
Work; remove only your own lock, when your work is finished and everyone is clear

ul: When several people work on the same isolated circuit, each fits **their own lock** to a **multi-lock hasp**. The supply cannot come back until the last lock is off.

A **whole-building shutdown** needs an agreed time, notice to everyone affected, and a plan for loads that must not lose power, such as fridges, servers, alarms and medical equipment. A UPS will only carry its load for a limited time, often minutes, not hours.
The **supply side of a main switch stays live** when the switch is off. Only JPS can make the service conductors dead.
Check for **other sources of supply**: a generator with an automatic transfer switch, solar PV, battery inverters and UPS units.
Bring lock-off devices that fit the breakers on that board. Plan for it: a breaker that cannot be locked is a problem to solve before the day, not on it.

Some workplaces control work on main switchboards and other high-risk systems with a **permit to work**: a signed form that says what may be done, by whom, when, and how the system has been made safe.

blocks.note: A tag warns; only a lock prevents. A plan that relies on a sign, a piece of tape or 'telling the office not to touch it' is not a safe isolation plan.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Count the items from the drawing and your survey: boxes, accessories, plates, fittings, breakers, isolators, fixings. Then measure the cable and conduit routes and add allowances.

flow: Measure each part of the route (board to first point, between points)
Add the drops down walls to each box
Add a length for each termination
Add an allowance for waste, usually 10 to 20%
Round up to the lengths or packs the supplier sells

blocks.p: **Worked example.** The route from the board is 14 m along the ceiling. There are three drops of 2.5 m (7.5 m), and you allow 0.3 m at each of 8 terminations (2.4 m). Total: 14 + 7.5 + 2.4 = 23.9 m. Add 15% for waste: 23.9 × 1.15 = **27.5 m** of each conductor. If the cable is sold in 30 m rolls, one roll of each colour is enough.
**Packs.** Always round **up**. If the job needs 26 saddles and they come in packs of 10, order 3 packs: 2 packs would leave you 6 short and stop the job.

blocks.p: Give the size, type and quantity of every item. 'Cable' or 'a breaker' on a list means someone will guess, and the wrong thing will arrive: the wrong size for the load, the wrong insulation for a wet place, or a breaker that does not fit the board.

Check the **voltage and frequency** on the rating plate before anything is bought. Most Jamaican circuits are 110 V or 220 V at **50 Hz**. Much equipment sold in the region is made for 60 Hz. Some works on both, but some 60 Hz motors run slower and hotter on 50 Hz, and clocks and timers keep the wrong time. If the plate does not say 50 Hz, check with the maker or supplier.

ul: Check what is already in the stores before you order.
Ask how long delivery takes. An item on back order can hold up the whole job.

If an item is not available, tell your supervisor and agree a substitute **in writing**: it must be equal to or better than the specification. Never force cables into a smaller conduit, or use a lower-rated part, because the right one has not arrived.

blocks.p: Check that each instrument is in date for calibration and that the leads and probes are in good condition when you book it, not on the morning of the job.

Cost = materials + labour + any other costs (equipment hire, transport), plus GCT at the current rate where it applies. **Worked example** (prices for teaching only): materials J$38,500; labour 6 hours at J$3,500 an hour = J$21,000; total before tax J$38,500 + J$21,000 = **J$59,500**.

blocks.note: Prices change often. Use the current price list or quotes from the supplier, and write the date of the prices on your estimate.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Break the job into steps and estimate each one from past jobs, time sheets or your supervisor's experience. Add them up, then add **contingency**: spare time for the small problems that nearly always turn up, such as hard concrete, a seized screw or a delivery that is late. 10 to 20% is common for routine work.

blocks.h: Fitting the work into the time allowed

blocks.p: When the client can only allow the power off for a short time, split the dead work into **stages** that each fit the window, and do all the work that does not need the circuit dead (fixing boxes, running empty conduit, preparing cables) outside the window. If the job needs 5 hours dead and the power can be off for only 2½ hours each evening, plan two evenings, and make sure the installation is safe and working at the end of the first one.

blocks.p: A bar (Gantt) chart shows each step against time, so everyone can see what should be finished by when, which steps overlap and where the hold points are. It is also the yardstick you measure progress against.

head: Trade
Agree
rows: Builders and plasterers
First fix is finished, inspected and recorded before walls are plastered.
Ceiling fixers
Cables and boxes are in, inspected and labelled before the ceiling boards go up; access panels where junction boxes must stay reachable.
Painters
Chases are made good before painting; plates and fittings go on after painting, so they are not painted over.
Air-conditioning installers and plumbers
Who fits the isolator, who connects the unit, who does the commissioning, and on which day.

ul: Share tasks by what each person can do **safely**, not by who is fastest or who complains least. Pair a new trainee with an experienced one.
Brief the team before work starts: the steps, who does what, the circuit that is isolated, the hazards and the controls. Ask questions to check they understood.
Stay close for the risky steps: isolation, work at height and connections. Correct unsafe acts at once and explain why.
Check work at the hold points, and give feedback at the end of the day.

blocks.h: Telling the client and the building's users

blocks.p: A shutdown notice should say: the date and time the power will go off and come back, which areas or circuits are affected, what people should do before it (save work, switch off computers, move food from fridges if needed), and who to contact. Give it in good time, and remind people on the day.

For work at weekends or out of hours, plan **access** (keys, gate, alarm codes, the security guard told), **help nearby** (no one works alone on electrical work), a phone, first aid, and who to call if something goes wrong.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, check the dates for school exams, church services, market days and holidays before you fix a shutdown. In the hurricane season, have a plan for leaving the site safe at short notice if a storm warning is given.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Monitoring, quality checks and dealing with change

blocks.p: Compare the work done with the schedule at **set times**: at the start of the day, at lunch and at the end of the day. Count something you can measure: boxes fixed, metres of conduit run, fittings connected. If the job is slipping, tell your supervisor early, while there is still time to bring in help or agree a new date. Bad news gets worse with age.
Plan the inspections and tests at the start, not at the end. Hidden work, such as cables above a ceiling or in a wall, must be inspected at a **hold point** while it can still be seen.

What it proves

Dead, before energising

No breakdown between conductors or to earth that could cause shock or fire
Dead, with sensitive equipment disconnected
Polarity

Dead, before energising

Correct voltage; GFCIs trip; everything works
Only after every dead test has passed

blocks.p: All readings go on a **test sheet** with the circuit, the instrument used, the date and the tester's name, so they can be checked later.

flow: Stop work on that part
Make it safe: isolate, lock off, tag, barrier if needed
Record what you found, with photos
Report to your supervisor, then the client, in plain words

Why it matters

The planned route blocked by a new beam or tank stand
Structural steel and concrete must not be drilled without the engineer's approval
Find another safe route and get it agreed
A breaker larger than the cable allows
The cable is not protected and can overheat
Report it; plan to correct it

blocks.h: Changes asked for by the client

blocks.p: Clients often ask for something different once work starts: a cheaper fitting, an extra light, a different position. Treat every change the same way: say what it involves, price the time and materials, and get it **agreed and recorded** (a written variation or change order, signed or confirmed by message) before you do it. If a request would break the code or the specification, say so politely, explain the danger, and offer a safe option.

blocks.note: Changes agreed by word of mouth are the most common cause of arguments over the bill at the end of a job. Write them down, even on a small job.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Final inspection of all the work
Dead tests completed and recorded
Tools counted; nothing left inside boards or boxes
Covers, blanks and plates fitted
Area cleaned and surfaces made good
Each person removes their own lock when everyone is clear
Energise with everyone told; carry out live checks
Update the board schedule and labels
Hand over and get the job card signed

blocks.p: The **board schedule** must show the new circuit and what it feeds, with any spare ways marked as spare. A board with a wrong schedule is a trap for the next electrician.

head: Include
Why
rows: What was done, where, on which circuits, and on which dates
A clear record of the work
Test results, or the test sheet attached
Proof the work is safe, for the client and the inspector
Defects found but not fixed, and why
The client knows what still needs attention
Advice, such as a circuit near its limit or an old board
Helps the client plan and stay safe
Changes agreed during the job
Matches the bill to what was agreed
Materials used and hours worked
For costing, and for planning the next job

blocks.p: Show the client what was done. Explain any new breakers, isolators and GFCIs, and how to test a GFCI with its button. Give them the updated board schedule, the test sheet and any makers' instructions and warranties. Answer their questions, then get the job card signed.

After the job, compare what happened with what was planned: time, materials, cost and quality. Ask what went well, what took longer than planned and **why**, and what was missing from the plan. The aim is a better next plan, not blame.

**Example.** A job planned for 6 hours took 8 hours: (8 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = **33%** over. The reason was harder concrete than expected, and only a light drill on site. Lesson for next time: on concrete slabs, book a rotary hammer drill and allow more time per fixing.

blocks.note: Keep your own record of how long common tasks really take: fixing a box in block, terminating a board, testing a circuit. Over a year it becomes your most accurate estimating tool.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can read a work order and say what is missing from it.
I can work out the current of a load with I = P ÷ V and decide whether a circuit can take more.
I can explain what a maker means by 'dedicated circuit', 'maximum breaker' and 'minimum circuit ampacity'.
I can deal with documents that disagree by getting a written ruling.
I can put competing jobs in order of priority.
I can carry out a site survey and record it with a sketch, measurements and photos.
I can write a method statement with the steps in a safe, logical order.
I can explain first fix, second fix, make good, hold point and contingency.
I can write a risk assessment and choose access equipment and PPE for a task.
I can write a safe isolation plan, including shutdowns, other sources of supply and multiple locks.
I can take off quantities, add allowances and round up to packs.
I can check that equipment suits a 110 V or 220 V, 50 Hz supply.
I can estimate time with contingency and draw a simple bar chart.
I can plan the work around the client and other trades, and write a shutdown notice.
I can share tasks in a team by what each person can do safely.
I can check progress against the schedule and plan the inspections and tests.
I can handle an unexpected problem or a client's change in the right order.
I can write a completion report, hand over, and review a job.

head: Figure or formula
What it is for
rows: I = P ÷ V; P = V × I
Current from power, and power from current
80% of the breaker rating
Most continuous load a breaker should carry under NEC rules (16 A on a 20 A breaker)
Usual waste allowance on cable, and usual contingency on time
Round up
Packs and rolls of materials
(actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100
Percentage overrun on time or cost
The JPS supply that equipment must match

terms: As-built (record) drawing
A drawing that shows the installation as it was really built.
Board (panel) schedule
The chart, usually inside the board door, listing each circuit and what it feeds.
Commissioning
Setting up equipment and proving it works as intended.
Contingency
Spare time or money in a plan for problems that usually turn up.
Continuous load
A load expected to run at its maximum for 3 hours or more.
Dedicated circuit
A circuit that feeds one item of equipment and nothing else.
First fix
Installing boxes, conduit and cables before the finishes; also called rough-in.
Hold point
A stage where work stops until it is inspected or approved.
Job card / work order
The instruction that starts a job and is signed off when it is finished.
Lock-off device
A device fitted to a breaker or isolator so a padlock can hold it off.
Make good
Repair disturbed surfaces so they are neat again.
Method statement
A written plan of the steps of a job, in order, and how each is done safely.
Multi-lock hasp
A clasp that takes several padlocks, so each worker can lock the same isolator.
Permit to work
A signed form that controls who may work on a high-risk system, when, and how it has been made safe.
Proving unit
A device that gives a known voltage, to show a tester works before and after proving dead.
Request for information (RFI)
A written question to the designer or client when documents are unclear or disagree.
Risk assessment
A written list of a job's hazards, who could be harmed and the controls.
Second fix
Connecting accessories, fittings and the board after the finishes; also called trim-out.
Site survey
A visit before planning to see and measure the real conditions.
Variation (change order)
A written, agreed change to the work, its price or its time.

c1.title: Outlets for a computer lab in Lucea
c1.text: Tajay Morrison, a Level 3 trainee, is planning a job at a high school in Lucea, Hanover. The work order reads: 'Install 8 double 110 V outlets in the computer lab for 8 desktop computers and one laser printer. Finish before end-of-term exams in three weeks.' The lab's board has two spare ways. Each computer takes about 150 W. The printer's data sheet gives 900 W when printing and says 'connect to a dedicated circuit'. The school will allow work only on Saturdays and after 3:30 p.m. on weekdays.

c2.title: An air-conditioning circuit at a Highgate credit union
c2.text: Electrician Mrs Claudette Rowe asks Level 3 trainee Andre Gordon to plan a new circuit for a split air-conditioner in the manager's office of a credit union in Highgate, St Mary. The unit's data plate reads: 220 V, 50 Hz; minimum circuit ampacity 16 A; maximum breaker 25 A. Connecting the new breaker means the whole main board must be dead for about two hours. The board also feeds the server cabinet, which runs through a UPS. The outdoor unit will sit on a bracket 3.5 m up the back wall, above the path to the staff car park.

c3.title: Staged rewiring at a Lacovia basic school
c3.text: Mr Desmond Bryan leads three trainees replacing the old wiring in a basic school in Lacovia, St Elizabeth: four classrooms and an office, each with its own circuits. Each classroom needs about 6 working hours with its circuits dead. Classes run from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., Monday to Friday, and the principal wants the work finished within two weeks without closing the school. The new cables go in chases cut in the block walls. Painters are booked to paint every room in the second week. One trainee, Kemar, joined the Centre last week.

c4.title: Surprises at a Discovery Bay guest house
c4.text: Trainee team leader Shanique Barrett and two trainees are replacing six ceiling lights and adding two outlets in a guest house at Discovery Bay, St Ann. The plan allowed one day. When they open the ceiling, they find a lighting cable chewed through by rats in two places, and an old outlet circuit with no earth (grounding) conductor. Later the owner asks them to add a light on the veranda that was not in the work order.

c5.title: Closing out a pump circuit in Grange Hill
c5.text: Trainee Rohan Clarke has finished a new 220 V circuit and isolator for a water pump at a farm shop in Grange Hill, Westmoreland. The plan allowed 6 hours of work and J$42,000 of materials. The job took 9 hours and J$47,500, because a water tank stand had been built across the planned cable route since the survey, and the cable had to take a longer way. All his tests passed. The owner, Mrs Henry, will run the pump herself.

questions.q: What does 'connect to a dedicated circuit' on the printer's data sheet mean for Tajay's plan?
o: The printer must be fed from a 220 V outlet in the lab
The printer needs a circuit that feeds nothing else
The printer outlet must have a GFCI of its own fitted
The printer must share a breaker with the lab lights
questions.why: A dedicated circuit has its own breaker and feeds one item only. Makers ask for it when a load is large or starts with a surge, so that other loads cannot overload the circuit or upset the equipment.

questions.q: About how much current will the 8 computers draw together?
o: About 1.4 A
About 13.6 A
About 19.1 A
About 10.9 A
questions.why: 8 × 150 W = 1,200 W, and I = P ÷ V = 1,200 ÷ 110 = 10.9 A. The 19.1 A figure wrongly adds the 900 W printer, which must have its own circuit anyway.

questions.q: The board has two spare ways. Which plan for the new circuits is best?
o: One new circuit for all 8 outlets and the printer
Use one spare way and feed the printer from the lights
One new circuit for the printer, one for the computers
Add the printer to the corridor outlet circuit
questions.why: The printer needs a dedicated circuit, and the computers' 10.9 A sits well inside a 20 A circuit with room to spare. All the loads together, about 19.1 A, would be above the 16 A the NEC allows for a continuous load on a 20 A breaker.

questions.q: Tajay estimates 16 hours of work, of which 5 need the lab's board dead. How should he plan it around the school's hours?
o: First fix on weekday afternoons; connections and tests on a Saturday
All 16 hours over the last weekend before the exams, working both days
Work through two school days while the classes carry on round the team
Fit everything in the afternoons, then test after the exams are over
questions.why: Work that does not need the board dead can be done in the weekday windows; the dead work fits a Saturday. That leaves time to put right any problem before the exams. Leaving the job to the last weekend, or the tests until after the exams, puts the deadline and safety at risk.

questions.q: Which breaker suits the air-conditioner's data plate?
o: A 30 A two-pole breaker
A 20 A two-pole breaker
A 20 A single-pole breaker
A 15 A two-pole breaker
questions.why: A 220 V load needs a two-pole breaker so both lines are switched together. It must not exceed the 25 A maximum on the plate, and it must not be below the 16 A minimum circuit ampacity, or it may trip in normal use. 20 A two-pole meets both.

questions.q: The main board must be dead for about two hours. What must Andre's plan include for the server cabinet?
o: Nothing, as the UPS will carry the server for the whole two hours
Leave the server breaker on and work around it with insulated tools
An agreed time with the manager, and a check of the UPS run time
Unplug the UPS first so its battery is not run down by the outage
questions.why: A UPS usually carries its load for minutes, not hours. The plan must agree the shutdown time with the manager and check the UPS run time, so the server can be shut down properly or kept running some other way. Working around a live breaker is not safe isolation.

questions.q: Why should Andre plan a lockable isolator (disconnect) beside the outdoor unit as well as the breaker in the board?
o: So the unit can be switched off at night to save power
So a technician can isolate it where he can see it
So the breaker in the board can be smaller than the plate says
So the outdoor unit runs on 110 V while the isolator is off
questions.why: Someone servicing the outdoor unit needs to isolate it within sight and lock it off, so nobody in the building can switch it on while they work. The NEC asks for a disconnect within sight of air-conditioning equipment.

questions.q: The outdoor unit is fixed 3.5 m up, above the path to the car park. Which control is most important in Andre's risk assessment?
o: Work fast at lunch time, when fewer staff walk along the path
Ask a staff member to shout a warning when people pass below
Stand the ladder on the sloping car-park ramp for extra height
Close the path with barriers and use a tower or tied ladder
questions.why: The hazards are a fall from height and tools or parts dropping on people below. Barriers keep people out of the drop zone, and a tower scaffold or a properly tied ladder gives a safe place to work. Relying on timing or a shouted warning does not control either hazard.

questions.q: Which sequence lets Mr Bryan rewire the school without closing it?
o: Switch off the main for two weeks and rewire every room at once
Do one classroom at a time, after classes, with only it dead
Do a little in all four classrooms each afternoon until all are done
Rewire the classrooms live while classes carry on in the other rooms
questions.why: Staging the work one room at a time keeps the rest of the school working, and doing it after classes keeps children away from the work. Working a little in every room leaves all four rooms half-finished and unsafe at once.

questions.q: Which job must the electricians finish in each room before the painters arrive?
o: Fit all the outlet plates and switch plates to the boxes
Switch on the new circuits and test each of them live
Fill and smooth the chases, ready for the paint
Take out the boxes so the painters have flat walls
questions.why: Making good the chases is the electricians' job and must be done before painting. Plates and fittings go on after painting, so they are not painted over, and circuits are energised only after the dead tests have passed.

questions.q: Mr Bryan estimates 30 working hours for the whole job and adds 15% contingency. About how many hours should the schedule allow?
o: 31.5 hours
45 hours
30.15 hours
34.5 hours
questions.why: 15% of 30 is 0.15 × 30 = 4.5 hours, so the schedule allows 30 + 4.5 = 34.5 hours. Contingency covers the small problems that usually turn up, such as hard block or a late delivery.

questions.q: Which task suits Kemar best on his first day with the team?
o: Locking off and proving the classroom circuits dead
Fixing boxes beside an experienced trainee
Terminating the new office board on his own
Testing the finished circuits for the test sheet
questions.why: A team leader shares tasks by what each person can do safely. Kemar can learn by fixing boxes under close watch. Isolation, termination and testing need skills he has not yet shown, and errors there can kill or leave hidden faults.

questions.q: What should Shanique do first about the cable the rats have chewed?
o: Keep that circuit locked off and photograph the damage
Wrap the bare places in tape so the day's plan stays on time
Finish the new lights first and mention it at hand-over
Switch the circuit on to see whether the lights still work
questions.why: Damaged cable with bare conductors can give a shock or start a fire. Keep it isolated, record it, then report it so a repair can be agreed. Taping over the damage hides it, and switching on could start a fire or shock someone.

questions.q: A trainee suggests joining the earth terminals of the old outlets to the neutral, as there is no earth conductor. Why is this dangerous?
o: It doubles the voltage at each of the old outlets in the room
It makes the breaker trip each time an appliance is started
If the neutral breaks, connected metal cases can go live
It makes each outlet draw current even when nothing is on
questions.why: Joined to the neutral, every metal case carries the neutral's voltage. If the neutral breaks or comes loose, the cases rise to full line voltage with nothing to trip. The fault must be reported and a proper remedy, such as a new earth conductor, agreed.

questions.q: What is the right way to handle the owner's request for an extra veranda light?
o: Fit it today without paperwork, since the owner is paying for the job
Refuse to do it, because it is not on the original work order
Fit it now, then add the cost to the bill at the end of the job
Price it and get it agreed in writing before fitting it
questions.why: Every change is priced and agreed in writing before the work is done, so there is no argument later about cost or time. Refusing outright loses a reasonable request; fitting first and billing later invites a dispute.

questions.q: With the rat damage and the missing earth, the one-day plan cannot be met. What should Shanique do?
o: Tell her supervisor now and agree a new plan
Keep quiet and work late until everything is finished
Leave the extra problems for another team to find later
Send the two trainees home and carry on by herself
questions.why: When a job is slipping, the leader reports early so the supervisor and client can agree extra time, materials or help. Working late without telling anyone leads to tired mistakes, and working alone on electrical work is unsafe.

questions.q: By what percentage did Rohan's job overrun its planned time?
questions.why: Overrun = (actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100 = (9 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = 50%. Dividing by the actual 9 hours instead of the planned 6 gives the wrong figure of 33%.

questions.q: In the job review, which lesson would most improve Rohan's next plan?
o: Allow 50% extra time on every job from now on
Order twice as much cable as each job needs
Check the route again shortly before ordering
Skip the survey on small jobs to save a day
questions.why: The overrun came from a site change after the survey. Re-checking the route just before ordering and starting would have caught it. Padding every job, or every order, by a fixed amount wastes money and does not deal with the cause.

questions.q: At hand-over, what should Rohan make sure Mrs Henry understands?
o: How the cable was sized from the code tables
How to switch off and lock the pump isolator
Which wire colours he used inside the board
How many metres of conduit the job used
questions.why: Mrs Henry will run the pump, so she must know how to isolate it safely, for example before a plumber works on it, and which breaker feeds it. Design details and colours belong in the records, not in her daily use.

questions.q: Which planning document sets out the work steps in order, with the tools and the isolation and testing method?
o: The method statement
The risk assessment form
The job card
The materials list
questions.why: The method statement says how the job will be done, step by step. The risk assessment lists hazards and controls, the job card says what is wanted and where, and the materials list says what to buy; a routine task needs all of them.
